doc.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Playing a seven-string guitar after George Van Eps
summary: Pizzarelli explains getting a seven-string Gretsch after hearing Van Eps, and other extra-string and tuning variations.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: We are filming today in Aspen, Colorado for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and it’s a great pleasure to welcome Bucky Pizzarelli, guitarist extraordinaire. I hate to tell you this but someone sold you a guitar with too many strings.
No I’ve had that for quite a while now you know, thanks to George Van Eps, a seven string, since ‘68, ‘69 I think, that’s when I started with it.
Was it a big adjustment at first?

It was. I was doing a lot of studio work and in the evenings I was doing The Tonight Show. And I went to Manny’s Music Store on 48th Street and bought a seven string Gretsch after I heard George Van Eps play it the night before in a night club. And I think about five or six guitar players in New York City all bought them the same day.
He made a big impression then. Is it always the lower string that’s added — on the seven string?

Well there are variations. Lenny Breau for instance has an extra string, only it’s a high string. And on the six string actually sometimes you tune it down to a D. This is a low A. And I’ve seen some tuned to low B flat.
That seems an odd note to put on the bottom of a guitar.

Yeah. An old friend of mine from Princeton, Bill Priestly, an architect from — a very good architect — from Chicago, had one, a seven string, in 1929, an old Martin, he just put an extra peg up there and put another string on.
